title: DPI TLS fingerprint causing intermittent control-plane reachability and leader thrash — investigation notes
content:
Summary:

During a 2026-03-27 on-call window we observed intermittent control-plane reachability losses for a single customer private deployment. Symptoms were short (10–40s) control-plane outages causing leadership re-election and transient RPC errors from the agent fleet. Incidents appeared correlated with a rolling change we deployed earlier that morning: a minor TLS client fingerprint tweak in the management agent (agent v2.14.1) intended to fix a compat issue with an upstream library.

Why this is unusual / context:
- Problem only affected one customer and started immediately after the agent push.
- Packet captures from both sides showed active TCP connections being abruptly reset mid-handshake (RSTs and occasional ICMP unreachable).
- Network path checks (traceroute, mtr) did not show classical routing flaps or asymmetric MTU issues.
- The customer's firewall appliance reported short-run DPI rule matches around the same timestamps.

High-level hypothesis that explains observations:
The customer's firewall DPI engine contains a heuristic/signature that matches on specific TLS ClientHello fingerprints / extensions. The agent TLS fingerprint change produced a ClientHello that the DPI engine flagged as "anomalous/unknown" and triggered a short-term active mitigation (TCP RST injection or short-lived connection drop). This caused control-plane gRPC/TLS sessions to fail briefly, triggering leader election and observable errors in the agent and control-plane logs.

Timeline (reconstructed):
- 2026-03-27 07:20 UTC: Scheduled rollout of agent v2.14.1 begins for customer A (canary hosts first).
- 2026-03-27 07:25 UTC: First control-plane connectivity error observed on canary. Alert page fired.
- 07:25–07:45 UTC: Intermittent RSTs on TLS handshakes observed in pcap from customer edge and from a nearby probe VM maintained by the customer.
- 07:30 UTC: Oncall attempted a configuration rollback for canary hosts; connectivity stabilized on rolled-back hosts.
- 07:40 UTC: Escalation to customer network team; their firewall logs show DPI rule id 0x5A3C matching TLS client hellos from our agent IP range.
- 07:50 UTC: Rollback completed cluster-wide; errors stopped.

Evidence collected:
- PCAP (customer-provided): server-side capture shows TLS ClientHello followed by injected RST within 150–400ms.
- Firewall logs (customer): DPI signature 0x5A3C triggered for client IPs running agent v2.14.1; action = "reset" (temporary).
- Agent logs: repeated gRPC TLS handshake failures with transient error codes.
- Internal rollout records: agent v2.14.1 changed TLS extension ordering + added a rarely-used extension A that matches the DPI heuristic.

Immediate mitigation taken:
1) Rolled back agent to v2.14.0 for affected customer: full rollback completed by 07:50 UTC.
2) Enabled temporary port fallback: agents reconfigured to allow control-plane on alternate TLS port 8443 for this customer until permanent fix applied.
3) Opened coordinated channel with customer's network team to share pcaps and firewall logs.

Root cause (narrow):
A management-agent TLS ClientHello fingerprint change triggered a DPI signature on the customer's firewall that actively resets TLS handshakes for matching fingerprints. The firewall's mitigation is aggressive (RST injection) and appears to be applied for short durations, leading to intermittent control-plane outages that look like network instability.

Contributing factors:
- Agent release changed TLS extension order / included uncommon extension without prior compatibility testing with customer middleboxes.
- We did not have an established compatibility test against customer's DPI signature set during canary.
- Customer firewall configured to treat unknown TLS fingerprint as high-risk and to actively drop/reset connections rather than passively log.

Longer-term fixes and action items (owner / ETA):
- Engineering: revert TLS extension A change and release v2.14.2 with an opt-in for the extension (owner: Martin Chen, ETA: 2026-04-01).
- Product/Security: create a pre-rollout compatibility checklist for managed-agent TLS changes that includes middlebox fingerprint risk assessment (owner: Sofia Alvarez, ETA: 2026-04-05).
- SRE: add a runbook section for "suspected DPI/middlebox reset" with specific triage steps (packet capture checklist, what firewall logs to request, probing guidance) and sample grep/pcap filters (owner: Aisha Patel, ETA: 2026-03-31).
- Support/SE: coordinate with customer to whitelist our management agent fingerprint OR apply firewall action change from RST to log for low-risk client IPs (owner: Ravi Kapoor, ETA: 2026-04-07).
- Telemetry: add metric/alert for elevated TLS handshake RST rate per-customer (>1% handshake RSTs over 5m) (owner: eng-observability, ETA: 2026-04-10).

Runbook notes / triage checklist (for oncall):
- If control-plane flapping is observed for a single customer immediately after agent rollouts, suspect middlebox interaction.
- Collect: agent version on affected hosts, precise rollout timestamps, full agent debug logs, tcpdump on agent host (client-side), and request server-side pcap from customer (if available).
- Correlate firewall logs: look for DPI signatures or actions around the handshake timestamps.
- Quick mitigations: rollback affected agent version; enable alternate TLS port if supported; temporarily add keepalive probes with lower frequency to reduce leader churn.
- Communication: notify customer network team and account manager; provide pcaps and explain suspicion of DPI signature match.

Customer communication draft (for CS to adapt):
- Short: "We observed short control-plane interruptions correlated with a recent agent update. After investigation we found your firewall DPI appliance was matching a new TLS fingerprint from our agent and injecting resets. We rolled back the agent and the issue stopped. We recommend either a short firewall rule change to avoid active resets for our management IPs or we can ship a minor agent update that restores the previous TLS fingerprint. Apologies for the disruption — attaching captures and logs for your team."

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is DPI signature 0x5A3C vendor-supplied default behavior or added by the customer's security team? (customer to confirm)
- Does the firewall keep an internal short-term blacklist for fingerprints it deems anomalous? Logs suggest yes but need confirmation of TTL behavior.
- Can we get a vendor-level description of what triggers 0x5A3C? Customer to escalate to vendor.

Post-incident retrospective notes:
- Risk profile: medium for customers who have aggressive DPI policies. Low to medium overall since problem surfaced only with a specific agent fingerprint change and only for customers running aggressive middleboxes.
- What went well: rapid rollback prevented wider disruption; good packet capture and firewall logs were available quickly because of previously established customer collaboration.
- What to improve: stricter pre-rollout testing with simulated DPI behavior, and a documented mitigation path (alternate port, fingerprint rollback) per-customer.

Attachments / artifacts location:
- PCAPs and firewall logs uploaded to internal incident folder: s3://redwood-incident-archives/2026-03/dpi-tls-ctrlplane-1298
- Jira task for agent revert and opt-in feature: JIRA-ENG-4331

Next steps (short):
- Engineering to prepare v2.14.2 revert build and coordinate with SRE for a controlled re-release (Martin).
- SRE to finalize runbook entries and add a short playbook for customer-facing comms (Aisha).
- Set up an observability alert for TLS-handshake-RST spike so we catch similar problems during future rollouts (eng-observability).

If anything else is discovered (e.g., vendor confirmation about DPI fingerprint behavior), add updates below and reopen the timeline log.
